summary: Defines the format of addresses used in XMPP, including support for non-ASCII characters. It updates RFC 3920 and is a proposed standard. It was later replaced by RFC 7622.

plainLanguage.summary: Chat users need addresses like email addresses. This explains what a correct one looks like, including names with letters from many languages.

subtitle: The format for identifying users and services in internet chat networks.

tldr.problem: XMPP needed a standard format for addresses used in chat systems that could support characters from all world languages, not just ASCII.
tldr.mechanism: A JID (Jabber Identifier) has three optional parts separated by @ and / characters: a localpart (like a username), a domainpart (the server), and a resourcepart (a specific connection or device). Each part is processed with stringprep, a Unicode normalization technique, to allow international characters while preventing security attacks.
tldr.outcome: XMPP systems can now consistently address users, chat rooms, and services worldwide using a simple text format that handles any Unicode text. RFC 7622 later replaced this with updated internationalization rules.

today: RFC 6122 defines the XMPP address format for chat systems that need to support international characters. It was obsoleted by RFC 7622, which uses the newer IDNA2008 internationalization standard instead of IDNA2003. However, the core address structure and stringprep processing approach remain the same.

sections.title: Addressing Protocol Entities in XMPP
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is a real-time communication system for instant messaging and presence information. The protocol needed a simple way to identify entities (users, chat rooms, services) on the network, similar to how email uses addresses like user@example.com.

XMPP's address format, called a Jabber Identifier (JID), has been used since the Jabber open-source community in 1999, and RFC 3920 standardized it in 2004. However, the 2004 standard relied on internationalization technology (IDNA2003) that later became obsolete. This RFC updates that standard to clarify the address format while IDNA evolves to the newer IDNA2008 approach.
sections.plainLanguage: Chat systems need addresses, just like email. This document explains the exact format so everyone's software agrees on what a valid address is, especially when it includes letters from different languages.

sections.title: The Three Parts of a JID
sections.content:
A JID is built from three parts in a fixed structure: [localpart@]domainpart[/resourcepart]. The localpart and resourcepart are optional, but the domainpart is always required. Each part is separated by an @ or / character.

The domainpart identifies the XMPP server and is the only required part; a JID can be just a domainpart. It must be a fully qualified domain name (like example.com), an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address (enclosed in square brackets), or an unqualified hostname. The localpart typically identifies a user account at that server (like romeo), making the full address romeo@example.com. The resourcepart names a specific connection or presence, such as home or phone, so a user can have multiple addresses like romeo@example.com/home for different devices.

Each part must be between 1 and 1023 bytes long after processing for internationalization, giving a maximum JID size of 3071 bytes including the separators. An implementation must identify the @ and / separator characters before applying any Unicode processing, because some Unicode characters decompose into these special characters.
sections.plainLanguage: A JID is like an email address with an extra part. You write user@domain or user@domain/phone. The domain is required, but you can leave out the user part or the phone part.

sections.title: Supporting Names from All Languages
sections.content:
For a global chat system, JIDs must accept letters and characters from any language. XMPP uses stringprep, a standardized process for preparing Unicode text so that addresses can safely include international characters. Stringprep applies three steps: character mapping (converting some similar characters to a standard form), Unicode normalization (arranging multi-part characters consistently), and prohibition of certain problematic characters.

The domainpart uses the Nameprep profile of stringprep, which is shared with domain names. The localpart and resourcepart each use special XMPP profiles called Nodeprep and Resourceprep. These profiles prohibit characters like @, /, and quotes that have special meaning in a JID structure. Stringprep ensures that café spelled as c-a-f-e-acute is treated as the same identifier as c-a-f-acute-e when both are processed.

XMPP servers must support Nameprep for domain names, and the Nodeprep and Resourceprep profiles for the localpart and resourcepart. Clients should support the same, though server support is required for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Languages use letters in many different ways. Stringprep is a recipe that says 'when you see this accent mark, treat it this way' so that café written two different ways counts as the same address.

sections.title: Security Risks and Protections
sections.content:
Because XMPP addresses can contain any Unicode character, two distinct characters might look nearly identical to a human reader. For example, the number one (1) and the lowercase letter L (l) look similar in many fonts, and a malicious user could register 1romeo@example.com to impersonate lromeo@example.com. More sophisticated attacks use Unicode characters that visually resemble familiar Latin letters, such as using Cyrillic or Cherokee characters in place of ASCII letters.

XMPP services can defend against this by restricting what scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Chinese, etc.) are allowed in a single localpart; a service might forbid mixing characters from different scripts in one address to prevent confusion. XMPP clients should also warn users when displaying an address that mixes scripts or uses unfamiliar characters. Additionally, end-to-end signing or authentication of stanzas can help ensure that a message truly comes from the claimed sender, even if a server has been compromised.

The RFC also notes that servers must validate the 'from' address on outgoing messages and that receiving servers must verify the sending domain to prevent address forging. While stringprep and Nameprep cannot prevent lookalike characters, responsible service policies and client UI design can mitigate the risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad actors could register a look-alike address that confuses people, like using a number 1 instead of the letter l. The best defense is for chat services to be picky about who can register similar addresses, and for chat programs to warn users when an address looks weird.

sections.title: Registering Stringprep Profiles
sections.content:
This RFC formally registers two new stringprep profiles with IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority): Nodeprep for processing XMPP localparts, and Resourceprep for processing resourceparts. These registrations allow other protocols that need similar string preparation rules to reference the same definitions, ensuring consistency.

The registration documents the character tables each profile uses from the base stringprep specification, the Unicode normalization form applied (Normalization Form KC for both), and the characters prohibited in the output of processing. Both profiles allow much of the Unicode character set but forbid special characters like @, /, :, <, >, and quotation marks that have protocol meaning in XMPP.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC officially tells the internet number authority 'we have two new recipes for preparing international text' so that other systems can use the same recipes if they need them.
